<reason>Both sides ran a tight, substantive debate, but CON built the sharper central frame — "who actually volunteers for the burden?" — and sustained it across rounds: children cannot independently consent, so the resolution's "genuinely voluntary" condition is structurally hollow for schools, and CON's badge analogy ("theology explains the rule, it doesn't redistribute the burden") directly rebutted PRO's structure/content defense. PRO's best material (the "proves too much" point on parental authority, and the doctrinal distinction between religious associations and ordinary employers) landed and kept the employer-side of the resolution defensible, but PRO never fully closed the children/schools gap, and conceded ground when framing volunteering as a family-level act — a concession CON exploited cleanly in both Rebuttal 2 and the closing. CON's closing crystallized the clash into one decisive question and quoted PRO's own language against it, which is more memorable and easier to adjudicate than PRO's closing, which mostly reasserted the associational-freedom frame without directly dissolving CON's consent objection. CON's Rebuttal 2 being clipped for length is a real execution cost, but the core content had already landed before the cutoff, so the damage is modest.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's "theology explains a rule, it does not redistribute the burden — that is precisely the badge, with better paperwork" (A4.2), combined with using PRO's own line "the volunteer unit is the family, not the girl" (B4.1) against them in the closing, was the most decisive exchange: it forced PRO's structural defense to concede that the person actually wearing the code never independently consented.</best_rebuttal>
